title: Tria capita ex opere quodam majori inedito de theoria lunae

deep.reconstruction:
This is the opening page of a posthumously printed chapter, 'On determining the Moon's place from lunar eclipses', from an unfinished larger treatise on lunar theory. Its problem is calibration. Once the theory has given formulas for the Moon's motion, the free constants have to be fixed from a few observed places: mean longitude at epoch, anomaly (perigee position), node longitude, and the true eccentricity. Euler's argument is that if the Moon really obeys the theory, then fitting these constants to a few observed places guarantees agreement at all times.

The calibrating data must give the true geocentric place without knowing the lunar parallax. The parallax itself is to be fixed only after the theory is confirmed. This rules out meridian transits and stellar occultations, since both are topocentric and need the parallax to be reduced.

Lunar eclipses are the ideal data. Entry into and exit from the Earth's shadow are physical events, seen simultaneously by every observer who can see the Moon, so they are free of parallax. At an eclipse the Moon is near opposition. If the instant of true opposition were known, the Moon's true longitude would follow at once: the Sun's longitude from solar theory plus 180°.

That instant is not observed directly. What can be timed are first and last contact, and for a total eclipse also the start of totality (immersion) and its end (emersion). Partial phases are measurable but less reliable because the shadow edge is fuzzy.

The neighbouring page carries the method forward on a spherical diagram (Fig. 205):
- S, s are the shadow-centre positions at first and last contact; L, l are the Moon's centre at those times.
- By symmetry SL = sl. At the outer contacts this equals α+β (umbral radius plus lunar semidiameter); at the inner contacts it equals α−β. The radii α and β need not be known.
- Motions are taken as uniform during the eclipse and counted relative to the node, so the shadow moves by (m+k)t and the Moon by (n+k)t.
- The instant sought is not the ecliptic opposition (σλ perpendicular to the ecliptic). It is the moment when ☊σ = ☊λ, i.e. the Moon's longitude measured in its own orbit equals that of the shadow centre. This avoids reducing the Moon's place to the ecliptic.

In modern terms this is the classical 'mid-eclipse gives syzygy' technique. It is recast as solving a small isosceles spherical configuration in node-relative coordinates.
errors: None on this page. Euler's claim that lunar eclipse contacts are free of observer parallax is correct, since the contacts are physical, simultaneous events.

On the next page the umbral radius is given as the sum of the lunar and solar parallaxes minus the solar semidiameter, with no atmospheric enlargement of the shadow (the usual ~1/50 correction). The symmetry SL = sl makes this harmless for the timing method, so it is not a real flaw.

ideas.what: Fixing the integration constants of a lunar theory (epoch, anomaly, node, eccentricity) by fitting a few accurate observed places
ideas.modern_name: Determining orbital elements / constants of the lunar theory from observations
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical practice: Ptolemy, Tycho, Mayer; Euler in his lunar theories
ideas.where_published: Euler, Theoria motus lunae (E187, 1753) and Theoria motuum lunae (E418, 1772), where constants are fitted to observations

ideas.what: Choosing lunar eclipses because they are free of parallax, so geocentric lunar places can be had without knowing the lunar parallax
ideas.modern_name: Use of eclipse observations for parallax-free lunar longitudes
ideas.usually_credited_to: Ancient (Hipparchus/Ptolemy used eclipse triples for the lunar anomaly)
ideas.where_published: Standard in 18th-century astronomy texts; unsure whether Euler printed it elsewhere

ideas.what: Symmetry of contact times (SL = sl) to locate the moment when the Moon's orbital longitude equals the shadow's longitude, using motions relative to the node
ideas.modern_name: Mid-eclipse / syzygy determination from symmetric contacts
ideas.usually_credited_to: Traditional eclipse computation; this node-relative orbital-longitude variant is a minor technical choice
ideas.where_published: E838 itself, Opera postuma 1862; unsure whether elsewhere

deep.surprise_reason: This is an introductory methodological page with standard, correct reasoning about why lunar eclipses are used to calibrate a lunar theory. The one slightly distinctive touch is using equality of node-distances, rather than ecliptic opposition, which avoids a reduction step. That is a convenience rather than a new result, and nothing here appears absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: The image reads 'ut nequidem ejus parallaxi sit opus' (one word, 'nequidem'), not 'ut ne quidem'.
The page header is the item number 'XVI.' and the chapter number is printed as dots ('Caput ....'), confirming that the chapter is an excerpt whose number was unknown to the editors.
